scenario: AITA for telling an intern to throw her banana peel in the trash? | A few details to set the stage: To get into my place of work, one needs to walk from the parking lot down a sidewalk that is along the side of the building. The other side of the sidewalk is semi-wooded with low growing evergreen shrubs. This sidewalk is about 100ft long, and has a trash can at either end. Also, in the last month, there have been a ton of flies buzzing around this area, so much so that the building manager called an exterminator. This morning, I (\~30s F) witnessed an intern (20s F) for one of the companies in our building walking into work eating a banana. About 3/4 of the way down the sidewalk, with a trashcan not even 25 feet away, she tossed the banana peel into the bushes. It landed on top of the bush and she just kept walking. I wasn't sufficiently caffeinated to be polite, so I blurted out "What the hell? There's a trash can right in front of you!" complete with the WTF hand gesture; pointing to the trash can. She ripped into me, claiming it's organic and feeds the animals. She was half yelling / half crying. I pointed at the peel sitting on top of the bush and told her to "pick up your (her) damn banana peel." Instead she cried loudly saying something unintelligible, got her peel, and put it in the trash. I'm thinking, great, this is over. Maybe she won't toss her banana debris into the bushes and we will have less flies. I'm sure I could have been more nice about it / sworn less, but I was just so shocked to see someone litter like that. I badged in to the building and she walked in behind me. At some point, she must have cried to her boss about it, because her boss found me today and asked if I confronted her intern. I said I had, then explained, as I have done here, about the banana peel. I guess she spent all morning crying about how "mean" I was and couldn't do any work. My brain was screaming "drama queen" but I apologized instead for upsetting the intern. We laughed together about absurdity of it all, especially over a banana peel! But now that it's the weekend and I'm sufficiently caffeinated, I'm wondering AITA for calling her out?

If you felt that consulting your family might have led to hesitation, pressure, or second-guessing that didn’t align with your inner truth, then going solo was likely the right move. Growth often happens outside of comfort zones, and you clearly prioritized your own well-being and autonomy. That said, the beauty of such decisions often reveals itself in hindsight. If I were in your shoes — valuing independence, needing a fresh start, and sensing that the timing was right — I’d hope I’d have the courage to do exactly what you did. Because sometimes, the most respectful thing we can do — for ourselves and, eventually, for our relationships — is to make hard choices with integrity, even if we make them alone. How has life in the new city treated you since the move?

prediction.raw: 0 You are not the asshole. Here’s why: While your delivery may have been brusque (and you acknowledge that you could have been more polite), your core action—calling out littering, especially in a shared space with an existing pest problem—was reasonable and justified. Banana peels, while organic, are not instantaneously biodegradable and can take weeks to decompose. In the meantime, they attract insects, rodents, and other pests—exactly the issue your building is already dealing with (flies). Tossing it onto a bush isn’t "feeding animals"—it’s littering, and it contributes to sanitation and aesthetic problems. The intern had two trash cans within easy reach (one just 25 feet away), so convenience wasn’t an excuse. Your frustration, though perhaps expressed more sharply than ideal, came from a place of concern for a shared environment. You didn’t insult her character or attack her personally—you told her to pick up her trash, which is a basic expectation in a professional setting. Additionally, the fact that her boss laughed about the situation with you suggests they recognized the overreaction. You apologized for upsetting her, which was gracious. Holding someone accountable for littering—even gently—is not being mean. It’s being a responsible member of a shared workspace. Could you have said it more calmly? Sure. But given the context, your reaction wasn’t out of line. You’re not the asshole.
